title: Solomon's lost songs and sayings need not have been inspired Scripture
source_text: VII. Quod spectat autem ad libros Salomonis, quorum plurimos interiisse constat, sciendum est non omnia, quae Prophetae & alii viri θεόπνευστοι scripserunt, authoritatem habuisse divinam: Nam, ut recte monet Augustinus de Civit. Dei lib. 18. Prophetae alia sicut homines scribere potuerunt, historica diligentia, & alia sicut Prophetae, inspiratione divina. Quae ita distincta fuerunt, ut priora quidem ipsis, posteriora Deo, per ipsos loquenti tribuenda fuerint. Ita ergo Salomon nonnulla quidem scripsit a Deo inspiratus, in quo genere sunt illi libri Salomonis qui partem Scripturae faciunt, & in Canonem sunt relati, veluti Proverbia, Ecclesiastes, & Canticum canticorum. Plurima vero scripsit idem ille propria industria, neque tanquam Propheta, sed tanquam vir omnium suo tempore doctissimus. In quo genere fuerunt multa physiologica, veluti quae scripsit de plantis a cedro usque ad hyssopum. Multa quoque ethica, quo pertinent parabolae illae quae proverbiorum libro non continentur. Denique multa poetica, ut illa quinque millia canticorum, de quibus loco citato mentio fit.
pass_a_gloss: As for the books of Solomon, of which it is agreed that very many have perished, it must be known that not everything which the Prophets and other θεόπνευστοι men wrote had divine authority. For, as Augustine rightly warns in City of God book 18, Prophets could write some things as men, with historical diligence, and other things as Prophets, by divine inspiration. These were so distinguished that the former are to be ascribed to them, the latter to God speaking through them. So Solomon wrote some things inspired by God — of which kind are those books of Solomon that form part of Scripture and are received into the Canon, such as Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. But very many things he wrote by his own industry, not as a Prophet but as the most learned man of his time. In that kind were many physiological matters, such as what he wrote of plants from the cedar to the hyssop; also many ethical matters, to which belong those parables not contained in the book of Proverbs; and finally many poetic things, such as those five thousand songs mentioned in the place cited.
pass_b_english: Yes, much of Solomon's writing is gone — but not everything a God-breathed man writes is divine Scripture.
Augustine in City of God 18: prophets can write as historians by human diligence, or as prophets by inspiration; only the latter bind as God's word.
Solomon's inspired share is what entered the Canon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs.
The rest — plant-lore from cedar to hyssop, extra parables, five thousand songs — can be brilliant human work without being lost canonical revelation.

choices.english: God-breathed men, not every writing therefore canonical
rejected: every jot they wrote is Canon
